items.stem: Which seismic waves are transverse and cannot pass through the Earth’s liquid outer core?
items.answer: S-waves
items.markingKey: D. Transverse waves cannot travel through liquids.

items.stem: Explain how seismic waves provide evidence that the Earth has a liquid outer core.
items.answer: S-waves are transverse and cannot travel through liquids; they are not detected in a “shadow zone” on the far side of the Earth from an earthquake, so part of the core must be liquid.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: S-waves are transverse and cannot travel through liquids; they are not detected in a “shadow zone” on the far side of the Earth from an earthquake, so part of the core must be liquid. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Light is a longitudinal wave because it travels in straight lines." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Light is transverse: its electric and magnetic fields oscillate at right angles to the direction of travel.
items.markingKey: Light is transverse: its electric and magnetic fields oscillate at right angles to the direction of travel. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: P-waves from an earthquake travel at 7.5 km/s. How long do they take to reach a seismometer 6000 km away?

Isabel stretched a slinky spring along a smooth floor to different lengths and measured the speed of a longitudinal pulse by video analysis.

Stretched length / m | Pulse speed / m/s: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
2 | 2.77 | 2.83 | 2.89
3 | 4.26 | 4.05 | 4.20
4 | 5.49 | 5.69 | 5.54
5 | 6.99 | 6.85 | 7.00
6 | 8.21 | 8.27 | 8.26

State the stretched length at which the repeat readings are least consistent, and calculate the range of the readings at that value. Suggest one way to make the data more reliable.
items.answer: 3 m; range = 0.21 m/s; e.g. take more repeats and discard anomalies / use more precise apparatus
items.markingKey: 1 3 m; 1 range = max − min = 4.26 − 4.05 = 0.21 m/s; 1 valid improvement (more repeats, more precise instrument, control a named variable).

items.stem: Amara plans an investigation into how the tension in a stretched slinky spring affects the speed of a longitudinal pulse along it. Describe how the results should be recorded, processed and presented, and explain how the reliability and validity of the conclusion will be judged.
items.answer: Results table with the independent variable (tension – the length the slinky is stretched to (2, 3, 4, 5, 6 m)) in the first column and repeat readings of the dependent variable with units in headings; calculate means (ignoring anomalies); plot a suitable graph of the mean dependent variable against the independent variable with a line of best fit; describe the trend and compare with the hypothesis; judge reliability from the spread of repeats and validity from how well variables were controlled.
items.markingKey: 1 table with IV, repeats and units; 1 means calculated, anomalies identified and excluded; 1 appropriate graph (line graph/scatter for continuous IV, bar chart for categorical) with line of best fit; 1 trend compared with hypothesis; 1 reliability (spread of repeats) and validity (controls) discussed.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "longitudinal wave".
items.answer: A wave in which the oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer, e.g. sound
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a wave in which the oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer, e.g. sound. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Diego writes: "In a sound wave, air molecules travel from the speaker to your ear." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Air molecules vibrate back and forth about fixed positions, passing energy along; they do not travel across the room.
items.markingKey: Air molecules vibrate back and forth about fixed positions, passing energy along; they do not travel across the room. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between a transverse wave and a longitudinal wave.
items.answer: In a transverse wave oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer (peaks and troughs); in a longitudinal wave oscillations are parallel (compressions and rarefactions).
items.markingKey: In a transverse wave oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer (peaks and troughs); in a longitudinal wave oscillations are parallel (compressions and rarefactions). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: In an investigation into how the tension in a stretched slinky spring affects the speed of a longitudinal pulse along it, state the dependent variable and describe how Alessia should measure it.
items.answer: speed of a pulse = distance travelled ÷ time, timed with video analysis over several reflections
items.markingKey: 1 mark for naming the dependent variable, 1 mark for a valid measuring method/instrument with unit: speed of a pulse = distance travelled ÷ time, timed with video analysis over several reflections.

items.stem: Using a “Mexican wave” in a football stadium as an example, explain transverse waves.
items.answer: Spectators stand up and sit down in turn and the wave travels around the stadium. Each person moves up and down (perpendicular to the direction the wave travels) without moving around the stadium.
items.markingKey: Context (Spectators stand up and sit down in turn and the wave travels around the stadium.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Each person moves up and down (perpendicular to the direction the wave travels) without moving around the stadium. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to transverse waves.

items.stem: Use a slinky spring to describe how you would demonstrate both a transverse and a longitudinal wave, and explain how each demonstration shows that energy, not matter, is transferred.
items.answer: Transverse: move one end side to side – coils move perpendicular to the wave direction; longitudinal: push and pull the end along the spring – compressions and rarefactions travel along. Tie a ribbon to one coil: it oscillates about a fixed point and does not travel along, while energy reaches the far end.
items.markingKey: Transverse: move one end side to side – coils move perpendicular to the wave direction; longitudinal: push and pull the end along the spring – compressions and rarefactions travel along. Tie a ribbon to one coil: it oscillates about a fixed point and does not travel along, while energy reaches the far end.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "wavelength (λ)"?
options: The change in direction of a wave when it passes into a different medium (or depth) because its speed changes
The speed of all electromagnetic waves in a vacuum, 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s
The number of waves passing a point each second, measured in hertz (Hz)
The distance from one point on a wave to the equivalent point on the next wave, e.g. crest to crest
items.answer: The distance from one point on a wave to the equivalent point on the next wave, e.g. crest to crest
items.markingKey: D. "wavelength (λ)" is the distance from one point on a wave to the equivalent point on the next wave, e.g. crest to crest.

items.stem: A student claims that waves with a higher frequency always travel faster. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: In a given medium speed is fixed; higher frequency means shorter wavelength (v = fλ).
items.markingKey: In a given medium speed is fixed; higher frequency means shorter wavelength (v = fλ). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why increasing the frequency of waves in a ripple tank decreases their wavelength.
items.answer: The wave speed in water of a given depth is constant; since v = fλ, if f increases λ must decrease in proportion.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The wave speed in water of a given depth is constant; since v = fλ, if f increases λ must decrease in proportion. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Tariq changed the frequency of the vibrating bar in a ripple tank (constant depth) and measured the wavelength by measuring 10 waves on the screen.

Frequency / Hz | Wavelength / cm: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
5 | 5.57 | 5.49 | 5.40
10 | 2.69 | 2.76 | 2.72
15 | 1.80 | 1.75 | 1.79
20 | 1.40 | 1.32 | 1.35
25 | 1.11 | 1.08 | 1.09

Describe the trend shown by the results and explain it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: Wavelength decreases as frequency increases; frequency × wavelength stays approximately constant. Wave speed depends on the water depth, which is constant, so v = fλ is constant and λ is inversely proportional to f.
items.markingKey: 1 trend: Wavelength decreases as frequency increases; frequency × wavelength stays approximately constant.; 1 use of data (quote means/values); 1-2 explanation: Wave speed depends on the water depth, which is constant, so v = fλ is constant and λ is inversely proportional to f.

items.stem: "Amplitude is the distance from a crest to a trough." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Amplitude is from the rest position to a crest (or trough) – half the crest-to-trough height.
items.markingKey: Amplitude is from the rest position to a crest (or trough) – half the crest-to-trough height. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Leila counts 16 waves passing the end of a pier in 15 s. The distance between neighbouring crests is 4.3 m. Calculate the frequency, the period and the speed of the waves.

Write a risk assessment for an investigation into how the depth of water in a ripple tank affects the speed of water waves. Identify two hazards, the risk each poses and how each risk will be reduced, and explain one ethical or environmental consideration.
items.answer: Key hazard(s): mop spills immediately – water near mains lamps; use low-voltage lamp. For each hazard: state what could go wrong, how likely/serious it is, and the precaution. Ethical/environmental: e.g. minimise waste and dispose of chemicals correctly, treat living organisms and volunteers with respect and consent.
items.markingKey: 2 two relevant hazards with the risk explained (e.g. mop spills immediately – water near mains lamps; use low-voltage lamp); 2 a specific precaution for each; 1 relevant ethical or environmental consideration.

items.stem: To what extent is it true that ripple tanks are the best way to teach wave properties?
items.answer: Ripple tanks are an excellent model but should be combined with simulations and other wave types.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: waves are visible and slow enough to measure; show reflection, refraction and diffraction clearly. Arguments against: water depth must be kept even, which is hard; measurements from shadows are imprecise; water waves differ from sound and light in some ways. Supported judgement: Ripple tanks are an excellent model but should be combined with simulations and other wave types. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The distance travelled by a wave per second; v = f × λ"?
items.answer: wave speed
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of wave speed.

items.stem: Explain how the wave equation v = fλ can be derived.
items.answer: In one period T the wave moves forward one wavelength λ, so speed = λ/T; since f = 1/T, v = fλ.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: In one period T the wave moves forward one wavelength λ, so speed = λ/T; since f = 1/T, v = fλ. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly explain why amplitude does not appear in the wave equation v = fλ.
items.answer: Wave speed depends on the medium, not on how much energy (amplitude) the wave carries; amplitude affects energy and loudness/brightness but not speed.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Wave speed depends on the medium, not on how much energy (amplitude) the wave carries; amplitude affects energy and loudness/brightness but not speed. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims that amplitude is the distance from a crest to a trough. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Amplitude is from the rest position to a crest (or trough) – half the crest-to-trough height.
items.markingKey: Amplitude is from the rest position to a crest (or trough) – half the crest-to-trough height. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Lars is investigating how the depth of water in a ripple tank affects the speed of water waves. Identify the independent variable in this investigation.
items.answer: depth of water (0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5 cm, measured with a ruler at several points)
items.markingKey: 1 mark: depth of water (0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5 cm, measured with a ruler at several points) (the variable that is deliberately changed). The measured variable scores 0.

items.stem: "Waves with a higher frequency always travel faster." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: In a given medium speed is fixed; higher frequency means shorter wavelength (v = fλ).
items.markingKey: In a given medium speed is fixed; higher frequency means shorter wavelength (v = fλ). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A displacement–distance graph of a wave shows crests 4 cm above the rest line and troughs 4 cm below, with crest-to-crest spacing 0.6 m. A displacement–time graph for one point shows one complete oscillation every 0.2 s. (a) State the amplitude, wavelength and period. (b) Calculate the frequency and wave speed. (c) Describe how both graphs would change if the frequency were doubled in the same medium.
items.answer: (a) 4 cm, 0.6 m, 0.2 s (b) f = 5 Hz, v = 3 m/s (c) speed unchanged, so λ halves to 0.3 m (twice as many waves on the distance graph); period halves to 0.1 s (twice as many oscillations on the time graph); amplitude unchanged unless energy changes
items.markingKey: (a) 1 amplitude 4 cm (not 8); 1 λ and T. (b) 1 f = 1/T = 5 Hz; 1 v = fλ = 3 m/s. (c) 1 λ halves; 1 T halves, v constant.

items.stem: A displacement–distance graph of a wave shows crests 3 cm above the rest line and troughs 3 cm below, with crest-to-crest spacing 0.6 m. A displacement–time graph for one point shows one complete oscillation every 0.1 s. (a) State the amplitude, wavelength and period. (b) Calculate the frequency and wave speed. (c) Describe how both graphs would change if the frequency were doubled in the same medium.
items.answer: (a) 3 cm, 0.6 m, 0.1 s (b) f = 10 Hz, v = 6 m/s (c) speed unchanged, so λ halves to 0.3 m (twice as many waves on the distance graph); period halves to 0.05 s (twice as many oscillations on the time graph); amplitude unchanged unless energy changes
items.markingKey: (a) 1 amplitude 3 cm (not 6); 1 λ and T. (b) 1 f = 1/T = 10 Hz; 1 v = fλ = 6 m/s. (c) 1 λ halves; 1 T halves, v constant.

items.stem: Which part of the electromagnetic spectrum is next to microwaves on the higher-frequency side?
items.answer: infrared
items.markingKey: D. Order of increasing frequency: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma.

items.stem: A student claims that gamma rays travel faster than radio waves because they have more energy. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: All EM waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum; gamma rays have higher frequency and shorter wavelength.
items.markingKey: All EM waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum; gamma rays have higher frequency and shorter wavelength. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between infrared and ultraviolet.
items.answer: Ultraviolet has a shorter wavelength and higher frequency than visible light and is ionising; infrared has a longer wavelength and lower frequency and is felt as heat.
items.markingKey: Ultraviolet has a shorter wavelength and higher frequency than visible light and is ionising; infrared has a longer wavelength and lower frequency and is felt as heat. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Mei placed a UV sensor under a clear plastic sheet coated with different numbers of thin layers of sunscreen and measured the UV intensity reaching the sensor under a UV lamp.

Layers of sunscreen | UV intensity / mW/cm²: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
0 | 3.99 | 4.01 | 3.97
1 | 1.73 | 1.74 | 1.78
2 | 0.79 | 0.77 | 0.79
3 | 0.35 | 0.36 | 0.37
4 | 0.16 | 0.16 | 0.16

Calculate the mean uv intensity when the layers of sunscreen was 1 .
items.answer: 1.75 mW/cm²
items.markingKey: M1 (1.73 + 1.74 + 1.78) ÷ 3; A1 1.75 mW/cm² (unit and sensible precision).

items.stem: Aiko is investigating how the distance from a Wi-Fi router affects the signal strength received by a phone. Identify the independent variable in this investigation.
items.answer: distance from the router (1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 m)
items.markingKey: 1 mark: distance from the router (1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 m) (the variable that is deliberately changed). The measured variable scores 0.

items.stem: Design a safe and valid method to investigate how the distance from a Wi-Fi router affects the signal strength received by a phone. In your answer include the variables, the equipment, the range and number of values of the independent variable, the number of repeats, safety and how the data will be recorded and processed.
items.answer: Place the router on a table in a long corridor; hold the phone at the same height; read signal strength at each distance after 10 s; take 3 readings at each distance on different days; plot strength against distance.
items.markingKey: MYP criterion B: 1 independent variable with at least 5 values in a sensible range; 1 dependent variable and how it is measured; 1 at least two controls and how they are controlled; 1 logical step-by-step procedure with equipment; 1 at least 3 repeats and calculation of a mean; 1 relevant safety point (Wi-Fi is non-ionising and low power; take care walking backwards in corridors). Model: Place the router on a table in a long corridor; hold the phone at the same height; read signal strength at each distance after 10 s; take 3 readings at each distance on different days; plot strength against distance.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "infrared radiation".
items.answer: EM radiation with wavelengths longer than visible red light, emitted by warm objects
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: EM radiation with wavelengths longer than visible red light, emitted by warm objects. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Distinguish between infrared and ultraviolet.
items.answer: Ultraviolet has a shorter wavelength and higher frequency than visible light and is ionising; infrared has a longer wavelength and lower frequency and is felt as heat.
items.markingKey: Ultraviolet has a shorter wavelength and higher frequency than visible light and is ionising; infrared has a longer wavelength and lower frequency and is felt as heat. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why infrared cameras can detect people in the dark.
items.answer: All warm objects emit infrared; people are warmer than their surroundings and emit more infrared, which the camera detects.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: All warm objects emit infrared; people are warmer than their surroundings and emit more infrared, which the camera detects. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: An EM wave has a frequency of 2.45 × 10^9 Hz. (a) Calculate its wavelength. (b) Identify the region of the electromagnetic spectrum it belongs to.
items.answer: (a) 1.22 × 10^-1 m (b) microwaves
items.markingKey: (a) M1 λ = c/f; A1 1.22 × 10^-1 m. (b) 1 microwaves.

items.stem: Briefly describe Wilhelm Röntgen’s discovery of X-rays (1895) and explain what it reveals about uses of X-rays.
items.answer: He noticed a screen glowing near a cathode-ray tube covered in card; an image of his wife’s hand showed her bones and ring. X-rays pass through soft tissue but are absorbed by dense bone and metal, producing a shadow image.
items.markingKey: Context (He noticed a screen glowing near a cathode-ray tube covered in card; an image of his wife’s hand showed her bones and ring.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: X-rays pass through soft tissue but are absorbed by dense bone and metal, producing a shadow image. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to uses of X-rays.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim that sunbeds should be banned for everyone under 18.
items.answer: The strong evidence of cancer risk justifies a ban for young people.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: UV exposure in youth greatly increases melanoma risk; Australia and Brazil have banned commercial sunbeds. Arguments against: personal freedom; some argue for vitamin D (although it can be obtained more safely). Supported judgement: The strong evidence of cancer risk justifies a ban for young people. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "diffraction".
items.answer: The spreading out of a wave as it passes through a gap or around an obstacle
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the spreading out of a wave as it passes through a gap or around an obstacle. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain the difference between reflection and refraction.
items.answer: In reflection the wave bounces back into the same medium at the same speed; in refraction it enters a new medium, changes speed and usually direction.
items.markingKey: In reflection the wave bounces back into the same medium at the same speed; in refraction it enters a new medium, changes speed and usually direction. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Mateo measured the speed of ripples in a ripple tank at different water depths.

Depth / cm | Wave speed / cm/s: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
0.5 | 20.1 | 19.9 | 19.6
1.0 | 27.2 | 28.9 | 28.0
1.5 | 35.5 | 33.3 | 33.8
2.0 | 40.9 | 39.1 | 39.4
2.5 | 44.9 | 46.0 | 44.3

State the depth at which the repeat readings are least consistent, and calculate the range of the readings at that value. Suggest one way to make the data more reliable.
items.answer: 1.5 cm; range = 2.2 cm/s; e.g. take more repeats and discard anomalies / use more precise apparatus
items.markingKey: 1 1.5 cm; 1 range = max − min = 35.5 − 33.3 = 2.2 cm/s; 1 valid improvement (more repeats, more precise instrument, control a named variable).

items.stem: A student claims that waves change frequency when they enter shallow water. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Frequency stays the same; speed and wavelength decrease.
items.markingKey: Frequency stays the same; speed and wavelength decrease. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Ripple tank models fully explain how light behaves."
items.answer: Ripple tanks are a useful analogy for wave behaviour but not a full model of light.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: show reflection, refraction and diffraction patterns similar to light. Arguments against: light is electromagnetic and transverse in a different way; light also behaves as particles (photons); ripple speeds and wavelengths are very different. Supported judgement: Ripple tanks are a useful analogy for wave behaviour but not a full model of light.

items.stem: When water waves move from deep to shallow water, what happens?
options: They slow down and their wavelength decreases
They speed up and their wavelength increases
items.answer: They slow down and their wavelength decreases
items.markingKey: C. Frequency stays the same, so λ falls with v.

items.stem: Distinguish between refraction and reflection.
items.answer: In reflection the wave bounces back into the same medium at the same speed; in refraction it enters a new medium, changes speed and usually direction.
items.markingKey: In reflection the wave bounces back into the same medium at the same speed; in refraction it enters a new medium, changes speed and usually direction. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Waves of frequency 10 Hz travel at 0.3 m/s in deep water and 0.225 m/s in shallow water. Calculate the wavelength in each region and state what happens to the frequency.
items.answer: deep 0.03 m; shallow 0.0225 m; frequency unchanged (10 Hz)
items.markingKey: M1 λ = v/f; A1 0.03 m; A1 0.0225 m; 1 frequency stays at 10 Hz (set by source).

items.stem: "A wider harbour entrance causes more diffraction." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Diffraction is greatest when the gap is similar to the wavelength; a much wider gap causes less spreading.
items.markingKey: Diffraction is greatest when the gap is similar to the wavelength; a much wider gap causes less spreading. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Design a harbour entrance to minimise waves inside a marina where the incoming waves have a wavelength of 8 m. Justify your design with reference to diffraction and reflection.
items.answer: A wide entrance (much larger than 8 m) lets waves pass straight through with little spreading, so a strong beam of waves reaches boats in line with the gap. A narrow entrance of similar size to the wavelength makes the waves diffract and spread their energy over a wide area, so wave height inside is much lower. Best design: a narrow, angled (offset) entrance so no moorings are in line with it, plus sloping or rough inner walls that absorb rather than reflect wave energy.
items.markingKey: A wide entrance (much larger than 8 m) lets waves pass straight through with little spreading, so a strong beam of waves reaches boats in line with the gap. A narrow entrance of similar size to the wavelength makes the waves diffract and spread their energy over a wide area, so wave height inside is much lower. Best design: a narrow, angled (offset) entrance so no moorings are in line with it, plus sloping or rough inner walls that absorb rather than reflect wave energy.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The maximum displacement of a point on a wave from its rest (equilibrium) position"?
items.answer: amplitude
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of amplitude.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "compression"?
options: A wave in which the oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer, e.g. sound
A region of a longitudinal wave where the particles are closer together than normal
The continuous range of electromagnetic waves arranged by wavelength or frequency: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma
A region of a longitudinal wave where the particles are further apart than normal
items.answer: A region of a longitudinal wave where the particles are closer together than normal
items.markingKey: B. "compression" is a region of a longitudinal wave where the particles are closer together than normal.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "EM radiation with wavelengths longer than visible red light, emitted by warm objects"?
items.answer: infrared radiation
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of infrared radiation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between diffraction and refraction.
items.answer: Refraction is a change in direction caused by a change in speed when entering a new medium; diffraction is spreading out through a gap or around an obstacle, with no change of speed.
items.markingKey: Refraction is a change in direction caused by a change in speed when entering a new medium; diffraction is spreading out through a gap or around an obstacle, with no change of speed. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between amplitude and wavelength.
items.answer: Wavelength is the distance between equivalent points on adjacent waves (horizontal on a graph); amplitude is the maximum displacement from rest (vertical).
items.markingKey: Wavelength is the distance between equivalent points on adjacent waves (horizontal on a graph); amplitude is the maximum displacement from rest (vertical). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why a cork floating on a pond bobs up and down but does not travel with the ripples.
items.answer: Water waves transfer energy, not matter; water particles (and the cork) oscillate about a fixed position as the wave passes.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Water waves transfer energy, not matter; water particles (and the cork) oscillate about a fixed position as the wave passes. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between non-ionising radiation and ionising radiation.
items.answer: Ionising radiation (UV, X-rays, gamma) has enough energy to remove electrons from atoms and damage DNA; non-ionising radiation (radio, microwaves, infrared, visible) does not, though it can heat tissue.
items.markingKey: Ionising radiation (UV, X-rays, gamma) has enough energy to remove electrons from atoms and damage DNA; non-ionising radiation (radio, microwaves, infrared, visible) does not, though it can heat tissue. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why you can hear someone talking around a corner but cannot see them.
items.answer: Sound wavelengths (about 0.3-3 m) are similar to the size of a doorway, so sound diffracts around it; light wavelengths are tiny (about 5 × 10⁻⁷ m), so light hardly diffracts.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Sound wavelengths (about 0.3-3 m) are similar to the size of a doorway, so sound diffracts around it; light wavelengths are tiny (about 5 × 10⁻⁷ m), so light hardly diffracts. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between wavelength and amplitude.
items.answer: Wavelength is the distance between equivalent points on adjacent waves (horizontal on a graph); amplitude is the maximum displacement from rest (vertical).
items.markingKey: Wavelength is the distance between equivalent points on adjacent waves (horizontal on a graph); amplitude is the maximum displacement from rest (vertical). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Rafael writes: "Light is a longitudinal wave because it travels in straight lines." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Light is transverse: its electric and magnetic fields oscillate at right angles to the direction of travel.
items.markingKey: Light is transverse: its electric and magnetic fields oscillate at right angles to the direction of travel. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "Mobile phones emit ionising radiation that causes cancer." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Phones use microwaves/radio waves, which are non-ionising; current evidence does not show they cause cancer at normal exposure levels.
items.markingKey: Phones use microwaves/radio waves, which are non-ionising; current evidence does not show they cause cancer at normal exposure levels. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Ana is investigating how the width of a gap in a barrier affects the diffraction of water waves in a ripple tank. Identify the independent variable in this investigation.
items.answer: gap width (1, 2, 3, 4, 6 cm), set with two metal barriers
items.markingKey: 1 mark: gap width (1, 2, 3, 4, 6 cm), set with two metal barriers (the variable that is deliberately changed). The measured variable scores 0.

items.stem:
Mateo changed the frequency of the vibrating bar in a ripple tank (constant depth) and measured the wavelength by measuring 10 waves on the screen.

Frequency / Hz | Wavelength / cm: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
5 | 4.37 | 4.32 | 4.33
10 | 2.21 | 2.12 | 2.19
15 | 1.41 | 1.48 | 1.48
20 | 1.06 | 1.08 | 1.09
25 | 0.85 | 0.84 | 0.88

Calculate the mean wavelength when the frequency was 15 Hz.
items.markingKey: M1 (1.41 + 1.48 + 1.48) ÷ 3; A1 1.46 cm (unit and sensible precision).

items.stem: With reference to the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, explain how it illustrates waves transferring energy, not water.
items.answer: An undersea earthquake off Sumatra sent waves across the ocean at around 700 km/h; they reached Sri Lanka about 2 hours later. In deep ocean the water mostly oscillated with small height while energy travelled vast distances; in shallow coastal water the energy produced huge waves.
items.markingKey: Context (An undersea earthquake off Sumatra sent waves across the ocean at around 700 km/h; they reached Sri Lanka about 2 hours later.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: In deep ocean the water mostly oscillated with small height while energy travelled vast distances; in shallow coastal water the energy produced huge waves. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to waves transferring energy, not water.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Wilhelm Röntgen’s discovery of X-rays (1895) shows uses of X-rays.
items.answer: He noticed a screen glowing near a cathode-ray tube covered in card; an image of his wife’s hand showed her bones and ring. X-rays pass through soft tissue but are absorbed by dense bone and metal, producing a shadow image.
items.markingKey: Context (He noticed a screen glowing near a cathode-ray tube covered in card; an image of his wife’s hand showed her bones and ring.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: X-rays pass through soft tissue but are absorbed by dense bone and metal, producing a shadow image. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to uses of X-rays.

items.stem: With reference to waves bending around headlands and into bays, explain how it illustrates refraction.
items.answer: Ocean waves approaching a coast at an angle turn to become nearly parallel to the shore. Waves slow in shallower water near the shore, so wavefronts bend until they arrive almost parallel to the beach.
items.markingKey: Context (Ocean waves approaching a coast at an angle turn to become nearly parallel to the shore.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Waves slow in shallower water near the shore, so wavefronts bend until they arrive almost parallel to the beach. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to refraction.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that ripple tanks are the best way to teach wave properties.
items.answer: Ripple tanks are an excellent model but should be combined with simulations and other wave types.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: waves are visible and slow enough to measure; show reflection, refraction and diffraction clearly. Arguments against: water depth must be kept even, which is hard; measurements from shadows are imprecise; water waves differ from sound and light in some ways. Supported judgement: Ripple tanks are an excellent model but should be combined with simulations and other wave types.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim that earthquake early-warning systems using P-waves are worth the cost.
items.answer: For earthquake-prone cities the benefits in lives saved outweigh the costs, though they complement rather than replace strong building codes.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: P-waves arrive before damaging S-waves, giving seconds of warning (e.g. Japan, Mexico); trains can be stopped and gas supplies shut off automatically. Arguments against: warning time is very short near the epicentre; false alarms reduce trust; expensive networks of seismometers. Supported judgement: For earthquake-prone cities the benefits in lives saved outweigh the costs, though they complement rather than replace strong building codes. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim that the benefits of using X-rays in medicine outweigh the risks.
items.answer: For a justified scan the diagnostic benefit is far greater than the small risk; scans should be used only when needed and doses kept low.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: diagnose fractures, dental problems and lung disease quickly; CT scans guide surgery and cancer treatment. Arguments against: ionising: small increase in cancer risk, especially with repeated CT scans; radiographers must be shielded. Supported judgement: For a justified scan the diagnostic benefit is far greater than the small risk; scans should be used only when needed and doses kept low. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: Hana investigated how the width of a gap in a barrier affects the diffraction of water waves in a ripple tank. The method had this weakness: the vibrator frequency was changed between gap widths. Evaluate how this weakness affects the validity of the results and suggest an improvement to the method.
items.answer: keep the frequency fixed so the wavelength is the same for all gaps
items.markingKey: 1 identifies how the weakness introduces error or an uncontrolled variable; 1 states the effect on the results/conclusion; 1-2 a specific, practical improvement: keep the frequency fixed so the wavelength is the same for all gaps

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "period (T)".
items.answer: The time taken for one complete wave to pass a point; T = 1/f
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the time taken for one complete wave to pass a point; T = 1/f. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which of these is a longitudinal wave?
items.answer: Sound in air
items.markingKey: C. Air particles oscillate back and forth along the direction of travel.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Radiation with enough energy to remove electrons from atoms, e.g. UV, X-rays and gamma rays"?
items.answer: ionising radiation
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of ionising radiation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why harbour walls are designed with narrow entrances.
items.answer: Waves diffract through the gap but lose energy as they spread out, so the water inside the harbour is calmer.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Waves diffract through the gap but lose energy as they spread out, so the water inside the harbour is calmer. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between frequency and period.
items.answer: Frequency is the number of waves per second (Hz); period is the time for one wave (s); f = 1/T.
items.markingKey: Frequency is the number of waves per second (Hz); period is the time for one wave (s); f = 1/T. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between a longitudinal wave and a transverse wave.
items.answer: In a transverse wave oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer (peaks and troughs); in a longitudinal wave oscillations are parallel (compressions and rarefactions).
items.markingKey: In a transverse wave oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer (peaks and troughs); in a longitudinal wave oscillations are parallel (compressions and rarefactions). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between ionising radiation and non-ionising radiation.
items.answer: Ionising radiation (UV, X-rays, gamma) has enough energy to remove electrons from atoms and damage DNA; non-ionising radiation (radio, microwaves, infrared, visible) does not, though it can heat tissue.
items.markingKey: Ionising radiation (UV, X-rays, gamma) has enough energy to remove electrons from atoms and damage DNA; non-ionising radiation (radio, microwaves, infrared, visible) does not, though it can heat tissue. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Lars writes: "A wider harbour entrance causes more diffraction." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Diffraction is greatest when the gap is similar to the wavelength; a much wider gap causes less spreading.
items.markingKey: Diffraction is greatest when the gap is similar to the wavelength; a much wider gap causes less spreading. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Aiko writes: "Amplitude is the distance from a crest to a trough." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Amplitude is from the rest position to a crest (or trough) – half the crest-to-trough height.
items.markingKey: Amplitude is from the rest position to a crest (or trough) – half the crest-to-trough height. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe a “Mexican wave” in a football stadium and explain what it reveals about transverse waves.
items.answer: Spectators stand up and sit down in turn and the wave travels around the stadium. Each person moves up and down (perpendicular to the direction the wave travels) without moving around the stadium.
items.markingKey: Context (Spectators stand up and sit down in turn and the wave travels around the stadium.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Each person moves up and down (perpendicular to the direction the wave travels) without moving around the stadium. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to transverse waves.

items.stem: Lars writes: "Gamma rays travel faster than radio waves because they have more energy." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: All EM waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum; gamma rays have higher frequency and shorter wavelength.
items.markingKey: All EM waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum; gamma rays have higher frequency and shorter wavelength. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims that a wider harbour entrance causes more diffraction. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Diffraction is greatest when the gap is similar to the wavelength; a much wider gap causes less spreading.
items.markingKey: Diffraction is greatest when the gap is similar to the wavelength; a much wider gap causes less spreading. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Lars writes: "Waves with a higher frequency always travel faster." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: In a given medium speed is fixed; higher frequency means shorter wavelength (v = fλ).
items.markingKey: In a given medium speed is fixed; higher frequency means shorter wavelength (v = fλ). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims that in a sound wave, air molecules travel from the speaker to your ear. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Air molecules vibrate back and forth about fixed positions, passing energy along; they do not travel across the room.
items.markingKey: Air molecules vibrate back and forth about fixed positions, passing energy along; they do not travel across the room. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With reference to the James Webb Space Telescope (launched 2021), explain how it illustrates infrared radiation.
items.answer: It observes in infrared to see light from the earliest galaxies and to look through dust clouds. Light from distant galaxies is stretched to infrared wavelengths, and infrared passes through dust that blocks visible light.
items.markingKey: Context (It observes in infrared to see light from the earliest galaxies and to look through dust clouds.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Light from distant galaxies is stretched to infrared wavelengths, and infrared passes through dust that blocks visible light. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to infrared radiation.

items.stem:
Yusuf measured the speed of ripples in a ripple tank at different water depths.

Depth / cm | Wave speed / cm/s: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
0.5 | 19.6 | 20.8 | 20.8
1.0 | 29.0 | 28.4 | 27.6
1.5 | 35.7 | 34.0 | 33.7
2.0 | 40.1 | 39.5 | 39.6
2.5 | 44.8 | 46.2 | 46.1

Describe the trend shown by the results and explain it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: Wave speed increases with depth, but less than proportionally (≈ √depth). In shallow water v ≈ √(g × depth); waves slow down in shallower water, which is why they refract at a depth boundary.
items.markingKey: 1 trend: Wave speed increases with depth, but less than proportionally (≈ √depth).; 1 use of data (quote means/values); 1-2 explanation: In shallow water v ≈ √(g × depth); waves slow down in shallower water, which is why they refract at a depth boundary.

items.stem: Seismometers 5000 km and 9000 km from an earthquake recorded P-waves (8 km/s) and S-waves (4.5 km/s). Calculate the time between the P- and S-wave arrivals at each station and explain how this difference allows scientists to locate an earthquake.
items.answer: 5000 km: 625 s vs 1111 s, gap 486 s. 9000 km: 1125 s vs 2000 s, gap 875 s. The gap increases with distance, so each station’s gap gives its distance; circles from three stations intersect at the epicentre.
items.markingKey: 5000 km: 625 s vs 1111 s, gap 486 s. 9000 km: 1125 s vs 2000 s, gap 875 s. The gap increases with distance, so each station’s gap gives its distance; circles from three stations intersect at the epicentre.

items.stem: "Ripple tank models fully explain how light behaves." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Ripple tanks are a useful analogy for wave behaviour but not a full model of light.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: show reflection, refraction and diffraction patterns similar to light. Arguments against: light is electromagnetic and transverse in a different way; light also behaves as particles (photons); ripple speeds and wavelengths are very different. Supported judgement: Ripple tanks are a useful analogy for wave behaviour but not a full model of light.
